label: GDP growth
source: National Treasury, Quarterly Economic and Budgetary Review
note: Whether the economy behind the borrowing is still expanding. Growth is what eventually pays debt down without new borrowing.

label: Reserves (import cover)
note: How many months of imports the reserves would cover. Well above the 4-month statutory floor and trending higher — a buffer that reduces near-term external financing risk.

label: Current account / GDP
source: National Treasury, Quarterly Economic and Budgetary Review
note: What the country earns abroad against what it spends there. A persistent deficit has to be financed, and financing it is what borrowing is for.

label: Fiscal deficit / GDP
note: How much the government spent beyond what it collected. Every shilling of deficit becomes new borrowing, raising the stock of debt that bond holders lend into.

label: Tax revenue / GDP
source: Kenya Revenue Authority, Annual Revenue Performance FY 2025/26
note: The share of national output the government actually collects in tax. Kenya's medium-term target is 20%. At 14%, every budget requires substantial borrowing to close the gap.

label: Debt service / ordinary revenue
note: Of every shilling collected in tax, about 69 cents went to debt service in FY 2024/25 before a single service was funded. This is the tightest measure of fiscal space — it deteriorates long before anything is missed.

label: Informal sector employment share
note: The share of jobs in the informal sector. At 83.8%, most Kenyans are outside the formal tax net — directly constraining revenue-to-GDP and the government's ability to close deficits without borrowing.

label: Net domestic borrowing
source: National Treasury, Parliamentary Budget Office Supplementary I Estimates FY 2025/26
note: How much the government borrowed from the domestic market in FY 2025/26 — revised up from the original KSh 624.7bn. Domestic issuance at this volume competes directly with private borrowers for available funds.
